paper_metadata.title: Effect of powder processing on microstructure and mechanical properties of a high-entropy Al24.2Si3.2Cu24.2Ti24.2Ni24.2 alloy

evidence.quote: A lightweight high-entropy Al 24.2Si3.2Cu24.2Ti24.2Ni24.2 alloy has been eﬀectively developed by sonication-assisted physical blending of micro-nanometre size particles followed by high-temperature sintering.

Equiatomic amounts of aluminium, copper, titanium and nickel, with a 3.25 atomic percentage of silicon particles (Al 24.2Si3.2Cu24.2Ti24.2Ni24.2), were added together in acetone containedin a glass beaker.

X-ray diﬀraction was conducted on an unsintered Al 24.2Si3.2Cu24.2Ti24.2Ni24.2 compact for reference purposes.
A physical blending of the metallic elements was done using a probe sonicator (VC-50, Sonics) for ten minutes.
The physically blended high-entropy alloy suspension was kept in an oven at 60° C for 12 h to evaporate the suspension media.
This was followed by subsequent compaction into preforms of 10 mm height and 10 mm diameter, at a pressure of 450 MPa using a uniaxial hydraulic press.

attributes.morphology: intermetallic compound layers on initial particle surfaces

evidence.quote: The diﬀusion process led to the formation of intermetallic compound layers on the initial particles surfaces, which might have proceeded inward to cover the entire particle considering their initial extremely ﬁne sizes.

However, the presence of some large patches of distinctive copper and nickel particle clusters suggests that the blending parameters, speci ﬁcally the blending duration, used in this study were apparently inadequate to break a few of the initial copper and nickel nanoparticles clusters.
The initial particles of the added elements were well bonded in the sintered Al24.2Si3.2Cu24.2Ti24.2Ni24.2 alloy (see Figure 3).
The relatively low value of the ultimate compressive strength of the sintered alloy could arise from the presence of nanopores in the microstructure (see Figure 5).

The diﬀused well-bonded sintered particles suggest mutual inter-diﬀusion between the elements in the alloy.

Hence, the sintering process resulted in the formation of multicomponent intermetallics in the evolved microstructure, instead of a solid solution, as can be seen in the X-ray diﬀraction spectrum (see Figure 2).

This high hardness value could be attributed to the formation of multicomponent intermetallics in the sintered microstructure, as intermetallic compounds are typically much stronger than their elemental counterparts even when in solid-solution form.

The presence of nanopores at the junction of the sintered particles with probable intermetallics makes the structure vulnerable to cracking easily, as indicated by the chip-o ﬀ pits on the polished sample surface, as shown in Figure 5.
